title: The month the museum was built

summary.text: Kernel Hive is a home lab that behaves like a museum. Inside one computer sit dozens of old, obscure and occasionally alarming operating systems, and they are not screenshots, and not an emulator you download and configure: they are <u>real machines, switched on right now</u>, their screens streamed into your browser tab, with a pointer and a keyboard that actually work. You download nothing and install nothing: you pick a machine off the wall and it is simply there, waiting where the last visitor left it. It began on 7 July 2026 with a private project, a single box under a desk, and twenty-four of these systems already running on it at once. The month that followed is the museum being built — machine after machine coaxed first into running unattended, then into being usable by a stranger who has never seen it before. It closes on 7 August 2026, the day the whole thing was published for anyone to read.

By the end of the month thirty-seven machines were open to visitors, plus [macOS](station:macos) and [RISC OS](station:riscos) as posters — illustrated wall placards standing in for machines not yet running. The workstations came first, the expensive kind nobody had at home: [Windows NT 3.51](station:nt351) and [NT 4.0](station:nt4) on full-size desktops, [OS/2 Warp](station:os2warp) at high resolution through IBM's own **GENGRADD** driver, [Solaris](station:solaris), and [OpenVMS](station:openvms) 9.2, a *2024* release still presenting the **DECwindows** Motif desktop. Microsoft's whole arc is here too, from [MS-DOS with Windows 1.01](station:msdoswin1) to a [Windows 11](station:win11) that installed itself without a single click, by way of [Windows 95](station:win95). Then the home computers: the *8-bit* [Commodore 64](station:c64), [Apple II](station:apple2) and [Amstrad CPC](station:amstradcpc), followed by the *68000* generation, [Amiga](station:amiga) and [Atari ST](station:atarist). The oddities earn their place: [Red Star OS 2](station:redstar2) and [Red Star OS 3](station:redstar3), North Korea's own desktop, kept strictly air-gapped; [TempleOS](station:templeos); and a [Multitech Microprofessor II](station:mpf2) from *1982* that has a keyboard and nothing else. Weeks then disappeared into [SGI IRIX](station:irix) on a *1993 Indy*, the machine that taught this project most of what it knows.

What you can do with them is the whole point. Move your mouse and the pointer moves; type and the letters land; drag a window, open a menu, go looking for whatever the makers left inside. None of these systems was built with a visitor in mind, so each needed its own arrangement. [Windows 95](station:win95), [TempleOS](station:templeos) and [OS/2 Warp](station:os2warp) each needed a small program installed inside them, listening for where you point, before the cursor would go there; [Solaris](station:solaris) could not take a pointer at all, and now it takes one. Type on a Finnish layout and the machine still receives what you meant, and on a phone an on-screen keyboard appears. You can watch a machine boot from cold, with sound, or skip the wait: [SGI IRIX](station:irix) wakes where it was left in five seconds, against six and a half minutes from cold. Every machine has an exhibit poster too — a written placard on what it was and why it mattered — and behind the **3D Museum** link the whole collection stands in one hall, sectioned by decade, that you can walk through.

Most of the month went into making this feel less like a remote control and more like sitting at the machine. The delay between moving your hand and the screen answering was cut hard. The picture now adapts to your connection instead of stalling on it, and joining a busy machine shows you its desktop straight away instead of grey. Typing is paced to each machine, after an *8-bit* computer quietly swallowed half a typed line. On a phone the whole vocabulary of a mouse had to be rebuilt out of fingers: tap, hold to drag, pinch to zoom, a badge to arm a right-click. And where an emulator itself was wrong, it was fixed and the fix published — including a mouse bug that could leave [SGI IRIX](station:irix) ignoring the pointer completely.

bullets: Microsoft's middle years fill a shelf of their own: [Windows 3.11](station:win311), [Windows 98 SE](station:win98se), [Windows 2000](station:win2000) and [Windows XP](station:winxp)
[Windows NT 3.51](station:nt351) still runs **Program Manager**; [NT 4.0](station:nt4) beside it wears the Windows 95 shell on the same kernel
[Windows 95](station:win95) has **Duke Nukem 3D** and **GTA** installed and launching; Windows 98 SE still has **Space Cadet** pinball
Three pocket Linuxes joined the wall: [Android](station:android), Jolla's [Sailfish OS](station:sailfishos), and [postmarketOS](station:postmarketos) of *PinePhone* mainline fame
[SerenityOS](station:serenityos) is a love letter to the late-*90s* desktop, written from scratch on camera, live on YouTube
[ToaruOS](station:toaruos) is one developer's UNIX with a real windowing compositor; [HelenOS](station:helenos) builds a whole desktop on message passing
[KolibriOS](station:kolibrios) is a complete graphical operating system written in pure assembly that fits on one floppy disk
[Tiny Core Linux](station:tinycore) is graphical Linux in about *16 MB*, with the whole system living in RAM
[ReactOS](station:reactos) is an open-source Windows 2000, reimplemented from scratch to run the same binaries
[Haiku](station:haiku) carries BeOS forward, yellow window tabs and all, and [AROS](station:aros) brings back the Amiga **Workbench** with none of the original code
[9front](station:ninefront) keeps Bell Labs' successor to Unix alive, where everything is a file and the file can be on another machine
[QNX Neutrino](station:qnx) is a hard-real-time microkernel whose **Photon** microGUI once held a whole desktop and a web browser
[Alpine](station:alpine) quietly runs half the containers on Earth; [FreeDOS](station:freedos) keeps a C prompt that never died
[Commodore 64](station:c64) and [Apple II](station:apple2) both run **GEOS** — a windows-icons-menus desktop on a *1 MHz* machine
[Amiga 500](station:amiga) arrives on **Workbench 1.3**, with the custom chips: *blitter*, *copper* and four-channel *Paula* sound
[Atari ST](station:atarist) boots **EmuTOS** into the *GEM* desktop, built-in *MIDI* ports and all
The [Microprofessor II](station:mpf2) has no software to load at all, so it comes with a program you type in yourself
[Windows 11](station:win11) began as a poster on the wall and was promoted to a machine you can sit down at
[Red Star OS 3](station:redstar3) reaches a logged-in desktop with no input at all: **KDE** on Fedora, reshaped in the DPRK to look like a Mac
The recorded cold boot of [SGI IRIX](station:irix) carries the *Indy*'s PROM startup chime, captured along with the picture
